class.name: BulletFlock2D
class.brief_description: Makes bullets fly as a flock: they avoid each other, line up and stay grouped (boids).
class.description:
Makes bullets fly as a flock (boids): they keep their distance from each other, line up with their neighbors and stay grouped, while each bullet keeps its own speed. One resource holds one flock's rules. Every physics tick each bullet looks at its flockmates and turns its heading toward a mix of three wishes, each with a strength per second: - [member separation]: turn away from flockmates closer than [member separation_range] (personal space; this is what makes bullets avoid each other and re-order instead of overlapping). - [member alignment]: turn toward the average heading of the flockmates within [member neighbor_range] (makes the swarm fly the same way, like a school of fish). - [member cohesion]: turn toward the center of the flockmates within [member neighbor_range] (keeps the swarm together instead of drifting apart). [b]How to use it:[/b] on a [BulletSpawner2D], open the Flocking group, turn on [member BulletSpawner2D.flock_enabled] and set [member BulletSpawner2D.flock] to a new BulletFlock2D. Turn on homing too ([member BulletSpawner2D.homing_enabled]) and you see the swarm right away: the defaults are tuned for that, for any sprite size. For a volley you spawned from the factory, call [method BulletVolley2D.flock_join]: [codeblock] var swarm := BulletFlock2D.new() swarm.separation = 15.0 # stronger personal space than the default 12 swarm.separation_range = 40.0 # a 40 px gap between bullet edges $Spawner.flock = swarm $Spawner.flock_enabled = true
# Or for a factory volley: var volley: BulletVolley2D = $BulletFactory2D.spawn_volley(data) volley.flock_join(swarm) [/codeblock] [b]Bullet size is counted for you.[/b] With [member count_bullet_size] (the default) the ranges are gaps between bullet edges, so the same flock works for 16 px and 128 px bullets, scaled ones included. Turn it off only if you want plain center-to-center pixels. [b]Give the swarm a reason to stay together.[/b] Flocking only turns bullets, it never changes their speed. A pattern that explodes outward (a big ring or a wide triangle) carries the bullets out of each other's [member neighbor_range] within a second, and then there is nobody left to flock with. A swarm looks alive when the bullets share a goal: turn on homing ([member BulletSpawner2D.homing_enabled]) so they chase the target together while separation keeps them apart, or fire a tight pattern (fan, aimed, small ring). [b]Recipes[/b] (start here, then tune): - [i]Swarm chasing the player:[/i] the defaults with homing on. They hold a clear gap between bullets while the swarm closes in; a strong separation spreads the arrival (bullets queue around the target), so lower [member separation] to about 6 when every bullet should hit fast. - [i]Orderly fish school:[/i] [code]alignment = 3, cohesion = 2[/code], the rest default. - [i]Bullets that only avoid each other[/i] (no grouping, no lining up): [code]alignment = 0, cohesion = 0[/code]. - [i]Tight ball that swirls:[/i] [code]cohesion = 5, alignment = 0.5, separation = 6, separation_range = 8[/code]. - [i]Wide, loose cloud:[/i] [code]separation_range = 80, neighbor_range = 300[/code]. - [i]Fair to dodge:[/i] add [code]max_turn_rate_degrees = 180[/code] so no bullet can whip around faster than half a turn per second. - [i]Leader-and-follower streams:[/i] [code]view_angle_degrees = 180[/code] (bullets only follow what is ahead of them). [b]How strong is "strong"?[/b] Each turn closes [code]1 - e^(-strength * delta)[/code] of the angle per tick, where strength is the length of the mixed wish (roughly the weights that are active). A strength of 1 turns a bullet about 63% of the way in one second, 3 in a third of a second. It never overshoots and looks the same at any frame rate. Weights from 1 to 20 are typical (the inspector slider covers them; type a larger value if you need one); much more than that snaps. [b]Who flies together[/b] is decided where the flock is armed ([member BulletSpawner2D.flock_scope], or the scope of [method BulletVolley2D.flock_join]); separate flocks never see each other. Edits reach every bullet already in flight on the next tick ([code]swarm.cohesion = 2.0[/code]). Every accepted change emits [signal Resource.changed]; a rejected value pushes an error and keeps the old one. [b]Mixing with other features:[/b] homing turns first and the flock bends the result. A spawner's homing turns at 5 per second by default ([member BulletSpawner2D.homing_smoothing]), which leaves the flock room; a homing that re-aims every tick ([member BulletVolleyData2D.homing_smoothing] 0) leaves it only a nudge. Wobble sways on top of the flock's heading; spin, bounce, graze, sound, pooling and time scale work as usual. A locked orbit owns the bullet's motion, and a direction curve in Override mode wins its axis. Frozen bullets are not flockmates, and nothing turns while the bullet world is frozen (time scale 0). [b]Limits:[/b] none hidden. The inspector sliders end at typical values but accept larger ones (type them in); a setter only refuses what has no meaning (negative or non-finite values, a [member neighbor_range] of 0, a [member view_angle_degrees] outside 0 to 360). [b]Cost:[/b] one pass per physics tick over every flocking bullet (an exact spatial hash grid), a few nanoseconds per flockmate looked at. [member max_neighbors] bounds the work per bullet and [member update_interval] spreads it over several ticks. Nothing is paid while no bullet flocks.

members.member: How strongly each bullet turns to fly the same way as its flockmates within [member neighbor_range] (per second). [b]Raise it[/b] (2 to 4) for an orderly school where everybody heads the same way; the swarm turns as one body. [b]Lower it[/b] toward 0 for a looser, messier swarm where bullets cross paths. 0 turns this rule off. Example: [code]alignment = 0[/code] together with [code]cohesion = 0[/code] keeps only the avoidance. Finite and >= 0.

How strongly each bullet turns toward the center of its flockmates within [member neighbor_range] (per second; it pulls harder the farther the center is, relative to the range). [b]Raise it[/b] (2 to 5) to keep the swarm in one tight blob that pulls stragglers back in; too high together with weak [member separation] makes bullets bunch up. [b]Lower it[/b] to let the swarm stretch and split into smaller groups. 0 turns this rule off. Finite and >= 0.

When on (the default), [member separation_range] and [member neighbor_range] are measured between bullet [b]edges[/b] instead of centers, so one setting fits every sprite: [code]separation_range = 24[/code] keeps a 24 px gap between 16 px bullets and between 128 px bullets alike, and bullets that overlap push harder than touching ones. A bullet's size is its drawn sprite ([member BulletVolleyData2D.texture_size], or the frame's size) times its own scale, so randomly scaled bullets keep their gaps too. Turn it off to measure plain center-to-center pixels (then size the ranges to your bullets yourself: [member separation_range] a bit more than one bullet's width). Costs about 10% more per flockmate check.

When on (the default), the bullet's sprite and collision shape turn with every flock turn, so arrows, fish and missiles always face where they fly. Turn it off for round bullets, or when the sprite should keep its own rotation while the flight path bends. Rotation data that spins the bullet owns the sprite and is left alone either way. A rotation that drives the heading ([member BulletVolleyData2D.adjust_direction_based_on_rotation], or homing that steers through the rotation) still follows the flock, or the flock's turn would be undone.

How many flockmates each bullet reads per tick, nearest first (0 = no limit). Lower values make big, dense swarms cheaper and slightly looser; the visual difference above about 16 is small. Example: [code]max_neighbors = 8[/code] for thousands of bullets packed together. The scan start rotates per bullet, so a capped flock does not drift to one side. Real starlings track about 7. A stack of N bullets costs exactly N x max_neighbors distance checks.

The fastest the flock may turn a bullet, in degrees per second (0 = no cap, the default). Use it to keep swarms fair to dodge: with [code]max_turn_rate_degrees = 180[/code] no bullet can reverse in less than a second, so the player can read the swarm. Lower values give wide, graceful curves; very low values (below about 45) make the rules too slow to matter. Homing and other steering are not capped by it.

How far a bullet sees its flockmates, in pixels: [member alignment] and [member cohesion] only consider flockmates closer than this. With [member count_bullet_size] (the default) it is the gap between the bullets' edges, so the default 150 works for any sprite size. [b]Larger[/b] (250 to 400) makes the whole swarm act as one big group (and costs a little more); [b]smaller[/b] (50 to 100) makes many small groups that ignore each other. If the bullets spread out farther than this, they stop flocking because nobody is in range. Finite and > 0.

How strongly each bullet turns away from flockmates inside [member separation_range] (per second). Closer flockmates push harder (weighted by [code]1 - gap / separation_range[/code]), so touching bullets push with the full weight and overlapping ones harder still. This is the "avoid each other" rule: it keeps bullets from overlapping and makes them re-order around each other. The default 12 holds a visible gap even against homing that turns at 5 per second (the spawner's default [member BulletSpawner2D.homing_smoothing]). [b]Raise it[/b] (15 to 20) for crisp personal space; [b]lower it[/b] (2 to 6) to let bullets brush past each other and reach a shared target sooner. It should usually be the strongest weight. Bullets stacked on the same spot part along a fixed direction per pair. 0 turns this rule off. Finite and >= 0.

Personal space in pixels: flockmates closer than this push the bullet away (see [member separation]). With [member count_bullet_size] (the default) it is the gap between the bullets' edges: the default 24 keeps about a 24 px gap whatever the sprite size. With it off, it is the distance between centers, so set it a bit larger than one bullet's width. [b]Larger[/b] spreads the swarm out; [b]smaller[/b] packs it tight. It is independent of [member neighbor_range] and may even be larger. 0 turns separation off.

Seconds between two steering updates of a bullet (0 = every physics tick, the default). Use it to make very large swarms cheaper: [code]update_interval = 3.0 / 60.0[/code] cuts the flock's cost to about a third with hardly a visible difference; values above about 0.2 s make the swarm react sluggishly. The updates are staggered across the flock so the work spreads evenly over the ticks; in between, every bullet keeps turning toward its last steering and still counts as a flockmate for the others. A bullet with no steering yet (a new or reused volley, a bullet woken from a freeze) computes at once.

Field of view in degrees, centered on each bullet's flight heading: flockmates outside it are ignored by every rule (and do not count toward [member max_neighbors]). 360 (the default) sees all around. 180 sees only what is ahead, which turns a loose swarm into leader-and-follower streams (bullets follow the ones in front and ignore the ones behind). Narrow cones (below about 90) make bullets mostly ignore each other. Stacked flockmates (same position) are always seen so a stack still parts, and a bullet with no heading sees all around. Between 0 and 360.

constants.constant: The bullets of one spawner flock together, every shot of it included (a second wave merges into the first). For [method BulletVolley2D.flock_join] on a factory volley: the factory's own volleys of this flock.
Every spawner and volley using this resource with this scope is ONE flock: bullets of several enemies merge into one swarm.
Each volley (one shot) is its own flock: waves pass through each other without reacting.
